Orchot Tzadikim 27:9: And our Sages of blessed memory already enumerated in Pirkei Avot (6:6) forty-eight things by which Torah is acquired. And whoever sets his heart on meriting the path of Torah should exert himself to fulfill those forty-eight things, and then he will rise to all good.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:10: And the student must be diligent and careful in his study, for the work of Torah is unlike other trades. For one who learns another trade, even if he is idle from it for several years, will not forget it. But when one studies Torah and does not review it, he forgets at once. And even if he reviews it a hundred times, if he lets his mind wander from it, he will forget everything. And this is only reasonable, for all other trades require the mind only when first learning the craft; but once performing it, they do not require the mind — one does his work while thinking of this and that. But study is not so, for each and every time his heart must direct itself to his lesson, and think of nothing else but his lesson. Therefore whoever lets his mind go idle immediately forgets what he toiled over all his days.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:11: And our Sages of blessed memory also said: if a person did not forget what he learned, he would have studied the entire Torah, and afterward would go about idle. And idleness brings on foolishness and transgression (Ketubot 59b). Therefore the decree of forgetting was made, so that a person occupy himself with Torah all his days, and through this not come to sin.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:12: And Torah brings a person to good deeds and merit, for when he occupies himself with Torah and is told of the punishment for transgressions and the merit of the commandments, he then takes it to heart to do good. And the toil of Torah makes him forget and keeps him from iniquity. But idleness drags along iniquity, and brings him down to Sheol. Therefore let him be diligent to occupy himself with Torah always, day and night, even when walking on the road or lying in his bed. And if he cannot study aloud, let him think in his heart about his lesson, and keep his mind on his study so that it not wander from his learning, and then he fulfills "and you shall meditate in it day and night" (Joshua 1:8). For it does not say "and you shall speak of it day and night" but "and you shall meditate in it," and meditation is only in the heart. And of this it is said, "and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up" (Deuteronomy 6:7, 11:19). And this is why our Sages of blessed memory were praised for never walking four cubits without Torah (Megillah 28a): either they were studying and reciting, or they were thinking in their hearts about their lesson or their study.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:13: Therefore devote your heart and all your mind to Torah at every time, for a person learns from Torah wisdom, proper conduct, humility and modesty, and all good deeds; and from Heaven his needs are provided for him, and the Torah guards him, raises him up, and exalts him, as the Sages taught (Mishnah Avot 6:1): Rabbi Meir said: whoever occupies himself with Torah for its own sake merits many things. And not only that, but the whole world is worthwhile for his sake. He is called "friend," "beloved"... and it raises him up and exalts him above all deeds. Behold, this is the fruit of its reward in this world, but for the World to Come: "no eye has seen it, O God, besides You" (Isaiah 64:3), and there is nothing above it for the World to Come. It is found in the Midrash (Ruth Rabbah 1:1): Rabbi asked Rabbi Betzalel: what is meant by what is written, "for their mother has played the harlot" (Hosea 2:7)? He said to him: when do the words of Torah become like a harlot? At a time when those who possess it demean it. How so? A sage sits and expounds "you shall not pervert judgment" (Deuteronomy 16:19), and he himself perverts judgment; "you shall not show favoritism" (ibid.), and he himself shows favoritism; "and you shall not take a bribe" (ibid.), and he himself takes a bribe.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:14: And so our Sages of blessed memory expounded: "and the wisdom of the poor man is despised" (Ecclesiastes 9:16) — what is the wisdom of a poor man that is despised? This refers to one who is poor in good deeds — then his wisdom is despised. And when he gives instructions to do good and does not do so himself, then his words are not accepted. And study is not the essential thing, but action (Mishnah Avot 1:4). Therefore every person should direct his deeds for the sake of Heaven. And see and understand from Elisha ben Avuyah, who, because his father taught him Torah not for its own sake, in the end turned to heresy. For we say in the Yerushalmi Chagigah (2:1) and in Midrash Kohelet (7:18): when he was circumcised, his father made a feast for the Sages, and invited our Sages: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua and the other Sages. And they were sitting at the feast speaking words of Torah until fire surrounded them. Elisha's father came and said to them: my masters, have you come to burn down the house?! They said to him: it is not so, but because we were reviewing the words of Torah, Prophets, and Writings, and the words testified among us that they were given from Mount Sinai, given from within the fire. He said: since I see that this is the power of Torah, if this son is established for me, I will give him to the Torah. But because his intent was not for its own sake but for honor, his son turned to heresy. Nonetheless, a person should always study even not for its own sake, for from [studying] not for its own sake one comes to [study] for its own sake (Pesachim 50b).
Orchot Tzadikim 27:15: And now I must write the matters of the Talmud and the commandments:
Orchot Tzadikim 27:16: All the commandments given to Moses at Sinai were given together with their explanation, as it is said, "and I will give you the tablets of stone, and the Torah, and the commandment" (Exodus 24:12) — "Torah" is the Written Torah, "and the commandment" is its explanation (Berachot 5a). And He commanded us to perform the Torah according to the commandment, and this commandment is what is called the "Oral Torah." Moses our teacher, peace upon him, wrote the entire Torah in his own handwriting before he died, and gave a scroll to each and every tribe; and he placed one scroll in the Ark as a witness, as it is said, "take this book of the Torah, and put it by the side of the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord your God, that it may be there as a witness against you" (Deuteronomy 31:26).
Orchot Tzadikim 27:17: And the commandment, which is the explanation of the Torah, he did not write, but commanded it to the elders and to Joshua and to the rest of all Israel, as it is said, "every word that I command you, you shall observe to do; you shall not add to it, nor diminish from it" (ibid. 13:1); and for this reason it is called "the Oral Torah." And from the days of Moses our teacher, peace upon him, until Rabbeinu HaKadosh, who is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, they did not compose a work to teach the Oral Torah publicly. Rather, in every generation the head of the court, or the prophet of that generation, would write for himself a record of the teachings he heard from his teachers, and would teach orally to the public. And so each and every one wrote for himself, according to his ability, from the explanation of the Torah and its laws as he heard them, and from matters newly derived in each generation regarding laws they had not learned by oral tradition but by one of the thirteen hermeneutical principles, and the Great Court agreed upon them. And so the matter continued always until Rabbeinu HaKadosh, who is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. And why did Rabbeinu HaKadosh do this, and not leave the matter as it was? Because he saw that the students were dwindling, and troubles were arising anew, and the Roman kingdom was spreading through the world and growing stronger, and Israel was being scattered to the far corners to be subjugated — when he saw this matter, that Israel was in confusion and Torah was being forgotten from Israel, he then composed the Mishnayot, to be in the hands of each and every person, so that they could study quickly and it not be forgotten. And he sat all his days, he and his court, and taught the Mishnah publicly. And before him were the great sages who received it from him, and with them thousands and myriads of the other sages. And the students of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi also composed works: Rav composed the "Sifra" and "Sifrei," to explain and make known the foundations of the Mishnah. And Rabbi Chiya composed the "Tosefta" to explain the matters of the Mishnah, and likewise Rabbi Hoshaya and Bar Kapara composed the Baraitot to explain the words of the Mishnah. And the matter continued in this way until the Amoraim came, and they had disputes in explaining the Mishnayot, Baraitot, and Toseftot, until Rabbi Yochanan composed the "Yerushalmi Talmud" in the Land of Israel, about three hundred years after the destruction of the Temple. And it is called "Yerushalmi" because he lived in Jerusalem. And afterward, about a hundred years later, Rav Ashi, who was in Babylonia, composed the "Babylonian Talmud." And the matter of the two Talmuds is the explanation of the words of the Mishnah and the elucidation of its depths, and matters newly derived in each and every court from the days of Rabbeinu HaKadosh until the composition of the Talmud. And from the two Talmuds, and from the Tosefta and from the Sifra and from the Sifrei and from the Toseftot — from all of them the forbidden and the permitted, the impure and the pure, the liable and the exempt, the invalid and the valid are explained, as they were transmitted from one person to another, back to Moses our teacher, of blessed memory, from Sinai.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:18: Also explained from them are matters that the Sages and prophets of each generation decreed, to make a fence for the Torah, as they heard explicitly from Moses our teacher, of blessed memory, as it is said, "and you shall keep My charge" (Leviticus 18:30) — make a guard for My charge (Moed Katan 5a). And so the customs and enactments that were instituted or practiced in each and every generation are explained from them, as the court of that generation saw fit. For it is forbidden to deviate from them, as it is said, "you shall not turn aside from the matter which they declare to you, to the right hand or to the left" (Deuteronomy 17:11). And likewise wondrous judgments and laws that were not received from Moses our teacher, of blessed memory, but were derived by the court of that generation using the hermeneutical principles by which the Torah is expounded, and the elders ruled and concluded that the law is thus — all of this Rav Ashi compiled in the Talmud, from the days of Moses until his own days.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:19: And after the court of Rav Ashi, who composed the Talmud and completed it in the days of his son, Israel was scattered throughout all the lands to an even greater extent, and reached the far corners and distant islands, and strife increased in the world, and the roads were disrupted by marauding troops, and the study of Torah diminished, and Israel no longer entered their study halls in the thousands and myriads as before. Rather, individuals gathered — the remnant whom the Lord calls — in every city and every province, occupying themselves with Torah, and understanding all the compilations of the Sages, and knowing from them the way of the law.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:20: After the Amoraim, the Geonim arose, who knew the entire Talmud — Babylonian and Yerushalmi, Sifra and Sifrei and Tosefta — and they brought to light the hidden things of the Talmud and explained its matters. Because the way of the Talmud is very deep, and further, it is in the Aramaic language mixed with other languages, since that language was clear to all in Babylonia at the time the Talmud was composed. But in other places, and in the days of the Geonim even in Babylonia, they did not know that language until they studied it. And many questions were asked by the people of every city to whichever Gaon lived in their days, to explain to them difficult matters in the Talmud, and they would answer them according to their wisdom. And those who asked would gather the answers and make books from them to understand from them. Also the Geonim of each and every generation composed works to explain the Talmud, some of whom explained individual laws, and some of whom explained tractates and orders. They also composed decided laws regarding the forbidden and the permitted, and the liable and the exempt, in matters the time required, so that they be accessible to the knowledge of one who cannot descend into the depths of the Talmud.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:21: [Continuation of the words of Rambam, of blessed memory, in his introduction to the Mishneh Torah]:
Orchot Tzadikim 27:22: "And this is the work of the Lord, which all the Geonim of Israel performed from the day the Gemara was composed until this time, the year one hundred and eight after the destruction of the Temple, which is the year four thousand nine hundred thirty-seven from the creation of the world.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:23: "And in this time the troubles have grown exceedingly severe, and the hour has pressed everyone, and the wisdom of our sages has been lost, and the understanding of our discerning ones has been hidden. Therefore those explanations, laws, and responsa that the Geonim composed, and which they saw as clear matters, have become difficult in our days, and only a few in number understand their matters properly. And there is no need to mention the Gemara itself, Babylonian and Yerushalmi, and Sifra and Sifrei and the Tosefta, which require a broad mind and a wise soul and a long time, after which the correct way in forbidden and permitted matters, and the rest of the Torah's laws, becomes known from them.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:24: "And because of this I, Moses son of Maimon the Sephardi, girded my loins, and leaned upon the Blessed Rock, and gained understanding in all these books, and saw fit to compose matters clarified from all these works, regarding the forbidden and the permitted, the impure and the pure, along with the rest of the Torah's laws. All of it in clear language and a concise manner, so that the entire Oral Torah be arranged in everyone's mouth, without difficulty and without resolution — not this one saying such-and-such and that one such-and-such, but clear, accessible, correct words according to the law that emerges from all these works and commentaries found from the days of Rabbeinu HaKadosh until now — until all the laws be revealed to the small and the great, in the law of every single commandment and in the law of all the matters the Sages and prophets instituted.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:25: "In sum: so that a person need not require any other work in the world for any law among the laws of Israel; rather, let this work gather in the entire Oral Torah together with the enactments, customs, and decrees made from the days of Moses our teacher until the composition of the Gemara, as the Geonim explained to us in all their works composed after the Gemara. Therefore I called this work 'Mishneh Torah,' since a person reads the Written Torah first and then reads this, and knows from it the entire Oral Torah, and need not read any other book between them." [Here end the words of the Rambam in his introduction.]
Orchot Tzadikim 27:26: And afterward Rabbeinu Moshe of Coucy arose and composed another book, gathering from that book of Maimonides and adding to it other matters of the later authorities. And so each and every one made a book according to the affairs of the generation he saw himself in. And so many rabbis composed decided rulings, such as: the Rokeach, and Rabbi Eliezer of Metz, and the Avi HaEzri, and Or Zarua. And so did many rabbis, each composing a book according to the affairs of the generation he saw himself in, for they saw that, because of our many sins, knowledge of the Talmud had diminished, and a person could not know it except through a book of decided rulings.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:27: And also Rabbeinu Shlomo, peace upon him [Rashi], who saw in his days the diminishing of hearts, that the generations, because of our many sins, were growing weaker and weaker, and therefore his heart was stirred to explain the Talmud, to teach the children of Israel understanding. And afterward his descendants arose — Rabbeinu Tam and Rabbeinu Yitzchak and the other rabbis — and engaged in great dialectic until they composed the "Tosafot" in the academy of Rabbi Yitzchak, the author of the Tosafot. And there were great ones there, such as Rabbeinu Shimshon of Sens, who also composed Tosafot, apart from the other students who were very numerous. And they were mighty in Torah, and their hearts were very great and open like a hall, and they studied with great intensity, and gave their souls over to the Torah, and knew, without study, the entire Talmud, the commentary [Rashi] and the Tosafot.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:28: And afterward, because of our many sins, troubles increased, and the academies diminished, and those later Tosafot became heavy upon them and they could not bear them. And other great ones came and abridged those Tosafot, each according to his own wisdom, to make study easier for the people of his generation. And still in those days they were expert in the entire Talmud, and knew the commandments from within the Talmud. Until it came about that they were expelled from France, where they held fast to the Torah and studied with great intensity, in the manner the early ones did in the days of the sages of the Talmud, whose essential study was to review the Talmud, in order to fulfill what they said: "and you shall teach them diligently to your children" (Deuteronomy 6:7) — that the words of Torah be sharp in your mouth; that if a person asks you something, you should not stammer and hesitate, but answer him at once (Kiddushin 30a). For this matter is impossible — that the commandments be sharp and ready in a person's mouth to answer the questioner — without much review, as they said (Chagigah 9b): one who reviews his chapter a hundred times is not equal to one who reviews it a hundred and one times.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:29: And we say (ibid. 9b) that Reish Lakish would review a law forty times before he came before Rabbi Yochanan. And so did everyone in the days of the sages of the Talmud, whose essential study was review. And we say (Megillah 7b): Rav Ashi was sitting before Rav Kahana. It grew light and the rabbis did not come. He said to him: why did the rabbis not come? He said to him: perhaps they were occupied with the Purim feast. He said to him: and could they not have eaten it the night before? He said to him: has the master not heard what Rava said: whoever eats the Purim feast at night has not fulfilled his obligation? Why? For it is written, "days of feasting and joy" (Esther 9:22) [implying daytime]. He said to him: did Rava say this? He said to him: yes! He studied it from him forty times, and it seemed to him as though it were placed in his pocket.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:30: And now see: this was a very light matter, and even so he reviewed it several times. And now there is no person who reviews such a matter more than once or twice. And there are great, clear proofs in several places in the Talmud that they were all accustomed to review, and each one had a fixed count of so many chapters per day, and when they were occupied during the day, they would make it up at night (Eruvin 65a). And every thirty days they would review their study. And in this manner they also studied in France, until they reached many virtues and great knowledge. And they had no need for books of decided rulings, for they knew the commandments from within the Talmud and the Tosafot. But from the day they were expelled from France, study diminished very, very greatly.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:31: And further, in this generation Torah has been forgotten, because these students suppose they are doing as the early ones did in holding fast to dialectical reasoning, but they are not at all comparable to the sages of France. For their heart was open like a hall, and their Torah was their trade, and they killed themselves over it day and night; therefore they attained and knew through their dialectic. But now they do not know it this way; rather, they confuse one another, and become idle most of the day, occupying themselves with that study for about half a day, and their study is a mere occasional occupation while their idleness is fixed. But in the days of the sages of the Talmud they went to study for ten years or more, and their study was greatly fixed, so that if one sneezed they would not say "bless you," because of the disruption to the study hall (Berachot 53a).
Orchot Tzadikim 27:32: From this matter one may know how fixed their study was. And we say (Ketubot 63a): Rav Yosef the son of Rava — his father sent him to the house of study before Rav Yosef, setting a term of six years. When three years had passed, the eve of Yom Kippur arrived, and he said: I will go and see the people of my household. His father heard, took an axe, and went out to meet him. He said to him: "have you remembered your dove?!" — and some say: "have you remembered your wife?!" He was so preoccupied [with study] that neither the master's term nor the other's term had ended. See and understand this matter, how attached they were to Torah, and therefore they merited the Holy Spirit!
Orchot Tzadikim 27:33: And so in the land of France they occupied themselves with great intensity and for a long time, and would sit in one place to study the entire Talmud, and would constantly review, and Torah never ceased from their mouths. And they did what the early ones did, as we say (Avodah Zarah 19a): a person should always recite, even though he forgets, and even though he does not know what he is saying. And they said (Shabbat 63a): first a person should learn, and then understand. And none of this is done now, for everyone wants to study Tosafot, and every novel insight and novel insight upon novel insight, before he even knows the form of the Talmud itself. If so, how can they succeed, since they do the opposite of what the sages of the Talmud said? For everything said in the Talmud is entirely true, and one cannot dispute it or change it, neither adding nor subtracting.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:34: And therefore, from the great toil of study, close reasoning, and dialectic, many abandon study because of the great toil of the teachings and the exactitude required to state them orally. For they say: how can we understand reasonings from the outside? Would that we knew what is within the books! And had they studied with fixed devotion day and night, they would have studied and become expert in the Talmud, and would have desired to study, for their hearts would have been able to understand easily; and a person would always come to study "sleeping yet not sleeping, awake yet not awake" (see Niddah 63a). And they would have added complete fear of Heaven through this, and the students would also have multiplied, and would have occupied themselves constantly with Torah. But now, because of the great toil of the teachings, the law has become like a heavy burden upon them, and they can no longer look at it, and through this they occupy themselves with madness and mockery, and confuse and become idle and occupy themselves with schemes of various kinds, and have no fear of Heaven.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:35: And they said in the chapter "HaSocher et HaPo'alim" (Bava Metzia 85a): Rabbi Zeira sat fasting for a hundred days, so that he would forget the Babylonian Talmud [he had studied], so that it would not disturb him [from the Yerushalmi]. And they said (Vayikra Rabbah 25:1): if a person stumbled in one transgression and became liable for death at the hand of Heaven, what should he do to live? If he was accustomed to read one page, let him read two pages; or to study a chapter once, let him study it twice; or to learn one chapter, let him learn two chapters. This teaches that much recitation is the essential thing; for if dialectic were the essential thing — to shout and raise one's voice half a day over a single statement — then it should have said: if he was at first accustomed to raise one difficulty, let him raise two difficulties.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:36: And in the chapter "HaIsh Mekadesh" (Kiddushin 52b) we say: when Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda said: let the students of Rabbi Meir not enter here, for they are contentious. And all this was because he did not want to be disturbed from his own recitation, for Rabbi Meir was sharp, and his colleagues could not fathom the full extent of his opinion (Eruvin 53a). And there it further says that Rabbi Yochanan said: the heart of the early ones was as wide as the entrance of the Temple hall, and that of the later ones as the entrance of the Sanctuary, and ours is like the eye of a fine needle. And Abaye said: and we are like a peg in a wall for the Gemara. And Rava said: and we are like a finger in wax for reasoning. And Rav Ashi said: and we are like a finger in a pit for forgetting.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:37: And now we, poor in understanding, cannot even say "like a finger," but rather "like a marble stone" for the Gemara and for reasoning. And regarding what is said in the chapter "Bameh Madlikin" (Shabbat 31a), Rava said: at the time a person is brought to judgment, they ask him: did you conduct business faithfully? Did you engage in dialectical reasoning in wisdom? — does this imply that a person must engage in dialectic? — This refers to the study of the Gemara, where we raise objections from Mishnayot against Baraitot and resolve them. Or else: through constant occupation and meditation on Torah, one's mind naturally becomes exact and finds its own reasoning. But to sit all day merely chattering — obviously one should not do this. And so now most students admit to themselves that they are not studying properly, and know they are not studying in the straight way, for from the great toil of their chattering they become completely idle, and fail to attain the study of Torah, Prophets, Writings, Aggadot, Mishnah, Midrashim, or any wisdom at all, because of their excessive stratagems.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:38: And our Sages expounded (Avot d'Rabbi Natan 24:6) on this verse: "I passed by the field of a lazy man, and by the vineyard of a man lacking sense; and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns, nettles had covered its surface, and its stone wall was broken down" (Proverbs 24:30-31) — whoever does not review his studies from the start confuses the chapter headings, and in the end confuses the words of the Sages, and in the end calls the impure "pure," and thus destroys the world. This teaches that whoever does not review his studies cannot rule properly, but errs in most of his rulings. And we say (Midrash Mishlei 10:1): Rabbi Yishmael said: come and see how difficult the Day of Judgment is! For the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to judge the entire world in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and when a Torah scholar comes before Him, He says to him: did you occupy yourself with Torah? He says to Him: yes! The Holy One, blessed be He, says to him: since you have admitted before Me, tell Me what you read and what you studied and what you heard in the academy. From here they said: whatever a person has read, let him hold onto it in his hand, so that shame and disgrace not overtake him on the Day of Judgment.
Orchot Tzadikim 28:1: Gate Twenty-Eight – The Gate of the Fear of Heaven
Orchot Tzadikim 28:2: It is written in the Torah: "and now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 10:12). And it is written (Isaiah 33:6), "the fear of the Lord is His treasure." And they said (Shabbat 31b): the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing else in His world but the fear of Heaven alone, as it is written (Job 28:28), "and He said to man, behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom" — fear is unique in the world (Rashi, ibid.); "behold" (hen) implies "one," for in the Greek language "one" is called "hen."
Orchot Tzadikim 28:3: And Rava said (Shabbat 31a): at the time a person is brought to judgment, they say to him: did you conduct business faithfully? Did you set fixed times for Torah? Did you occupy yourself with being fruitful and multiplying? Did you hope for salvation? Did you engage in dialectical reasoning in wisdom? Did you understand one thing from another? And even so: if the fear of the Lord is his treasure — yes; if not — no. A parable of a man who told his messenger: "bring up for me a kor of wheat to the attic." He went and brought it up for him. He said to him: "did you mix in a kav of preservative for it?" He said to him: "no." He said to him: "it would have been better had you not brought it up at all." And Rabbah bar Rav Huna said (Shabbat 31a-31b): any person who has Torah in him but no fear of Heaven is like a treasurer who was given the keys to the inner chambers but not the keys to the outer ones — by which door shall he enter?
Orchot Tzadikim 28:4: Rabbi Yannai proclaimed: woe to him who has no courtyard yet makes a gate for the courtyard. The meaning of "darta" is "courtyard," and "tar'a" is "gate." And Rabbi Yannai came to say: whoever has no courtyard, what benefit is there for him in making a gate for nothing? So Torah is only a gate through which to enter into the fear of Heaven. And Rava said to the rabbis (Yoma 72b): I beg of you, do not inherit a double Gehinnom — to be weary and toil in Torah in this world and not fulfill it, and inherit Gehinnom at your death; and in your lives you did not enjoy this world because of the toil of study, and at your death you will lose the World to Come as well.
Orchot Tzadikim 28:5: And since we see that everything depends on the fear of Heaven, and that the entire Torah is of no benefit to a person except through the fear of Heaven, and it is the peg on which everything hangs, and it alone stands for a person forever and ever. And so David, of blessed memory, testified (Psalms 19:10), "the fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever." And so King Solomon, peace upon him, testified and said (Ecclesiastes 3:14), "and God has made it so that men should fear before Him." And it is written (Proverbs 15:16), "better is a little with the fear of the Lord, than great treasure and trouble with it."
Orchot Tzadikim 28:6: Therefore you must know that there are three kinds of fear. The first is a very inferior fear, such as a person who does not fear before God, but when he does some good deed, he does it because of people: for if he does not do the good deed, whether in study, in charity, in prayer, or in anything else, then they will not believe in him and will disgrace him — so whatever he does is only to find favor in their eyes. And if this man intends this all his days, then his end is destruction, since his thought is not directed to the Holy One, blessed be He.
Orchot Tzadikim 28:7: The second: he fears before God, but he fears Him because of the punishment of Gehinnom, or lest he not come to the Garden of Eden, and through this he strengthens himself in good deeds. And this man, even if he fulfills the whole Torah with this intent — it is good that he fears the Holy One, blessed be He, bringing him to judgment, but he has not attained the essence of the good, for his entire intent in his service is only for his own benefit, not for the honor of the Holy One, blessed be He.
Orchot Tzadikim 28:8: But the third, the fine pearl, is one who fears before the Holy One, blessed be He, not because of anything in the world, but because he trembles before Him, and all his limbs shudder when he remembers His greatness and His might. And because this matter is very, very deep for people to understand, for it is the way of people not to do their deeds unless they hope for some benefit or that harm be kept from them, and if neither of these applies, then the deed is to them vanity and emptiness.
Orchot Tzadikim 28:9: And because this third level is hard to attain, it was permitted to perform the commandments out of fear of punishment and hope of reward. Therefore you find blessings and curses to frighten the heart of the reader so that his heart be awakened, just as is done for a child, since he is small in wisdom, awakening his heart by giving him nuts and fruits. And it turns out the child does not study for the honor of the Torah, since he does not know its worth and does not know the good in his studying, but thinks of study as toil and labor, and toils and studies in order to attain the fruits, like one who performs a trade that is not important in his eyes except for the profit in it.
Orchot Tzadikim 28:10: But if they promised a small child, saying to him: study and I will give you a beautiful wife, or a house, or you will be king — he would not study for this, and his heart would be awakened more for a single piece of fruit than for all of these, since his heart does not recognize the benefits of a wife or a kingship. And so is the matter of the Torah: to awaken a person's heart with things he recognizes and knows to be good, to draw his heart to do good. And all this must be done for a person because his wisdom is small and weak, and he has no discernment to discern the secret of the matter, and this is called "not for its own sake." Therefore do not be like a child, but seek truth for the honor of truth. And this matter requires great understanding and discernment.
